intro: The finale of the Symphony No. 6 in B minor “Pathétique”, Op. 74, marked Adagio lamentoso, opens with a violin melody whose notes pass between the two violin sections; neither plays it complete. After the G-major close of the preceding march, the movement returns to B minor and ends in that key.

sections.label: A · Falling melody divided between violins
sections.mNote: First and second violins share the falling tune.

sections.label: B · D-major melody, violins and violas
sections.mNote: Violins and violas play a descending melody over horns.

sections.label: B · Orchestra, descending scales
sections.mNote: Fast descending scales bring the D-major tune to its climax.

sections.label: A′ · B-minor lament theme returns, strings
sections.mNote: The strings play the opening melody again.

sections.label: A″ · Strings, approach to F♯
sections.mNote: The lament theme builds to a sustained dominant in the bass.

sections.label: Link · Low-brass chorale
sections.mNote: Trombones and tuba enter after the single tam-tam stroke.

sections.label: B′ · Broad melody in B minor
sections.mNote: The broad melody returns over the double basses’ low B.

relations.label: The contrasting melody is restated
relations.basis: The Andante contrasting group expands by restating its broad melody. Both excerpts lie in that group before the first large withdrawal, not in the later B-minor coda. CENS diagonal mean 0.939, sustained 38.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 51 s (cache/form/tchaikovsky-6-finale.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

relations.label: The opening lament returns
relations.basis: The opening lament returns after the contrasting melody and its withdrawal. The later excerpt agrees with the return marked near 316 s, while changed surrounding texture prevents an unchanged-section claim. cues.title: Divided melody, first and second violins
cues.text: The first and second violins play alternate notes of a falling melody. Neither part contains the whole tune. The opening chord is a half-diminished chord in B minor, the symphony’s home key.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 16, reproduces the divided melody. Opening harmony: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky). https://qso.com.au/uploads/QSO-Learning-Resource-Breathtaking-Tchaikovsky-1-.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Vladimir Davydov, 1893
cues.text: On 23 February 1893, months before he orchestrated the symphony, Tchaikovsky told Vladimir Davydov that the finale would be “a long drawn-out adagio”. In the same letter he wrote that he felt blissfully sure he could still compose.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky to Vladimir Davydov, letter 4865, 11/23 February 1893. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Symphony_No._6

cues.title: Second theme in D major
cues.text: The first violins and violas play a broad new melody in D major over a horn accompaniment, and the trombones answer it. The tune moves downwards in long phrases.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 17, describes the horns, strings and trombone answer. D-major second theme: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First performance, Saint Petersburg, 1893
cues.text: Tchaikovsky conducted the first performance in Saint Petersburg on 28 October 1893. Two days later he wrote to his publisher, Jurgenson: “It’s not that it displeased, but it has caused some bewilderment.” He added that he was more proud of it than of any of his other works.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky to Pyotr Jurgenson, letter 5062, 18/30 October 1893, quoted in Tchaikovsky Research’s account of the first performance, 16/28 October 1893. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Symphony_No._6

cues.title: Climax in descending scales
cues.text: The broad Andante tune speeds up and spreads across the full orchestra. Its climax comes in fast downward scales. The descending line, first played quietly by the violins, now passes through the whole ensemble.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 17: the Andante grows in passion and speed, reaching its climax in downward scales. https://qso.com.au/uploads/QSO-Learning-Resource-Breathtaking-Tchaikovsky-1-.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the opening theme
cues.text: The strings bring back the opening melody. Its falling phrases are extended as the rest of the orchestra takes them up, building to another climax.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 17, describes the return and expansion of the opening theme. https://qso.com.au/uploads/QSO-Learning-Resource-Breathtaking-Tchaikovsky-1-.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Vladimir Davydov, 1893
cues.text: On 14 August 1893, while he was still scoring the symphony, Tchaikovsky wrote to his nephew Vladimir Davydov that it was “the most sincere of all my creations. I love it as I have never loved any of my other musical offspring.” Davydov was its dedicatee.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky to Vladimir Davydov, letter 4998, 2/14 August 1893, quoted in Tchaikovsky Research’s composition history; dedication on the title page of the autograph score. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Symphony_No._6

cues.title: Tam-tam stroke and brass chorale
cues.text: A single tam-tam stroke follows the climax. After a long hold on F♯, the dominant of B minor, trombones and tuba play a chorale.
cues.evidence: Tam-tam, dominant harmony and low-brass chorale: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky). Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 17, includes the chorale score.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the second theme, B minor
cues.text: The broad melody returns, now in B minor. Muted strings descend over a repeated low B in the double basses. The theme was first heard in D major.
cues.evidence: The transformed second theme, muted strings and final B-minor resolution are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky). Low-B bass pulse: Harlow Robinson, https://www.bso.org/works/tchaikovsky-symphony-no-6.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Death of Tchaikovsky, 1893
cues.text: Tchaikovsky died of cholera at a quarter past three on the morning of 6 November 1893, nine days after the première, in his brother Modest’s flat in Saint Petersburg. Twenty days after the première, Eduard Nápravník conducted the symphony in a memorial concert.
cues.evidence: Alexander Poznansky’s account of Tchaikovsky’s last illness and death, 25 October/6 November 1893 (Tchaikovsky Research, Tchaikovsky: A Life); the memorial performance under Nápravník in Harlow Robinson’s Boston Symphony programme note. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Tchaikovsky:_A_Life https://www.bso.org/works/tchaikovsky-symphony-no-6

cues.title: Close in the cellos and basses
cues.text: The final descent passes into the cellos and double basses. The symphony ends in their low register, with B minor still sounding.
cues.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 17, describes the bassoons, cellos and basses at the close, https://qso.com.au/uploads/QSO-Learning-Resource-Breathtaking-Tchaikovsky-1-.pdf. Harlow Robinson describes the thinning close at https://www.bso.org/works/tchaikovsky-symphony-no-6.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Bassoon line to the D-major Andante
transitions.from: A · Falling melody divided between violins
transitions.to: B · D-major melody, violins and violas
transitions.how: A descending bassoon line dies away over horns and strings. At the Andante the first violins and violas take up a new melody in D major, with the horns in support. The melody moves broadly downwards, and the trombones follow it.
transitions.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 17; D-major key: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky). https://qso.com.au/uploads/QSO-Learning-Resource-Breathtaking-Tchaikovsky-1-.pdf

transitions.title: Return of the opening string theme
transitions.to: A′ · B-minor lament theme returns, strings
transitions.how: The climax of the Andante breaks into fast descending scales and dies down. The strings then play the opening melody again in B minor, in long falling phrases.
transitions.evidence: Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Symphony No. 6 learning resource, p. 17, describes the downward scales and the return of the opening theme. https://qso.com.au/uploads/QSO-Learning-Resource-Breathtaking-Tchaikovsky-1-.pdf

transitions.title: F♯ pedal into the brass chorale
transitions.how: The climax holds F♯ in the bass and its force gradually falls away. A single tam-tam stroke sounds as it dies down, and quiet trombones and tuba take over with a chorale. Their chords round off the dominant harmony before the last return of B minor.
transitions.evidence: Dominant pedal, tam-tam and chorale: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky). Chorale score reproduced in Queensland Symphony Orchestra’s learning resource, p. 17.

transitions.title: Second melody returns in B minor
transitions.to: B′ · Broad melody in B minor
transitions.how: After the low-brass chorale, muted strings play the broad second melody again, now in B minor. Double basses pulse on low B underneath. The other instruments stop one by one, and the falling phrases pass to the lower strings.
transitions.evidence: Second-theme return and final scoring: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._6_(Tchaikovsky); Harlow Robinson, Boston Symphony programme note, https://www.bso.org/works/tchaikovsky-symphony-no-6.

source.title: Tchaikovsky, Symphony No. 6, Op. 74, miniature score (Leipzig: Ernst Eulenburg, [1928], plate E.E. 3892)
source.locator: IV. Finale, printed pp. 185–208 (bars 1–170); bar numbers placed between the file’s section times

timeline.note: Divided violins trade the falling lament; flutes and bassoons double softly.
The winds and strings play a crescendo to fortissimo, then fall away.
A wind trio and a bassoon line lead out of the lament over soft strings.
D-major Andante: broad string melody, repeated horn notes, clarinet and bassoon.
Woodwind play repeated notes; horns, trumpets and trombones answer in a crescendo.
The climax is for full orchestra, fortissimo, with timpani; the violins play runs.
After the climax, winds, horns and strings drop back to piano.
The lament returns in the strings, with bassoons and horns.
Stringendo: winds, horns and trumpets drive the strings upward.
Pesante: trombones, tuba and timpani join; marked and heavy in fortissimo.
F♯ held and dying away. Winds, horns, low brass and timpani fade.
A quiet trombone and tuba chorale, with the single tam-tam.
B minor: muted violins and wind chords over the basses’ low pulse.
The wind instruments stop; a bassoon plays a line over the low strings.
Only cellos and basses remain, fading to pianissimo.

composer.epithet: Composer who could write a brilliant ballroom scene and, within it, a single melody showing that someone present was unhappy.
facts: School of Jurisprudence; Saint Petersburg Conservatory, 1862–65, with Anton Rubinstein and Nikolai Zaremba
Nadezhda von Meck: an allowance, 1877–90, and a friendship conducted by letter
Three ballets; Eugene Onegin, The Queen of Spades and other operas
composer.background:
At Kamenka on 6 July 1878, Tchaikovsky was explaining to Nadezhda von Meck how he composed. Ideas came to him in the middle of conversations, and he kept them in his head until he could sketch them on the first sheet of paper to hand. He held that waiting for the right mood was no way to work. “Inspiration is a guest who does not like to visit the idle,” he told her. He then stopped for dinner. At two o’clock he resumed, and went on to sketching, orchestration, fair copies and how far a symphony must keep to its traditional form.

He was born in Votkinsk, where his father managed an ironworks. He grew deeply attached to his French governess, Fanny Dürbach, and began piano lessons at the end of 1845. The profession chosen for him was the law. In 1850 he entered the preparatory class of the Imperial School of Jurisprudence in Saint Petersburg. Four years later his mother died of cholera. He graduated in 1859 and took a post at the Ministry of Justice, while giving more and more of his time to opera and concerts.
